idiom_name: public method composed of private method calls
implementation_notes: The coordinator is a public method whose body only calls private methods; class members are private by default in C#, and Microsoft's guidance is to keep the narrowest access level that makes sense, which is what keeps the steps out of the class's contract. Use this form when several members share a step or when subclasses should be able to replace it (widen to protected deliberately).
pitfalls: A step left internal (or protected) by omission or convenience becomes part of the assembly's or derived types' contract; the default private is what keeps the seam narrow.
Local functions (the C# 7 realization) are private by definition and cannot be reached from elsewhere - do not choose them for a step that another member must call.

A step that returns Task turns the coordinator into an async method and every call into an await; the sequence then interleaves with other work and an exception surfaces at the await instead of at the call.

variants.name: Local functions nested in the caller (C# 7)
variants.idiom_name: method body that declares and calls local functions
variants.implementation_notes: C# 7 local functions let the steps be declared inside the coordinator: they see its arguments and locals, cannot be called from anywhere else, and - unlike lambdas - are converted to a delegate only when used as one, so the ordinary call case allocates nothing. Use them for steps that exist for one method only and need its locals; keep private methods when a step is shared across members, must be overridden, or would make the coordinator too long to read.
pitfalls: Declaring a local function static whenever nothing is captured avoids the compiler-generated closure class; the default capturing form lifts captured variables into a heap allocation.
Local functions cannot be declared inside an expression-bodied member, so a => coordinator must become a block body before its steps can move inside.
Capturing this, or a loop variable, inside a local function that later becomes a delegate keeps the object (or the last value) alive - the local-function analogue of a closure leak.
